reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / GOLD & ATS guidelines
clinicalPearls: ABPA is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus colonising the airways, occurring almost exclusively in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis
Suspect it in poorly controlled asthma with recurrent exacerbations, fleeting pulmonary infiltrates, and expectoration of brownish mucus plugs
Markedly elevated total serum IgE and Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG, with peripheral eosinophilia, support the diagnosis
A positive immediate skin test or specific IgE to Aspergillus reflects the underlying sensitisation
Imaging classically shows central bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction, sometimes with transient infiltrates
Treatment centres on suppressing the immune and inflammatory response with corticosteroids, with antifungal therapy used to reduce fungal burden in selected cases
The disease evolves through stages including acute presentation, remission, exacerbation, and, if untreated, fibrotic end-stage lung disease
It is a hypersensitivity phenomenon rather than tissue-invasive infection, distinguishing it from invasive aspergillosis and aspergilloma
reference.pathophysiology: In predisposed patients, inhaled Aspergillus fumigatus spores germinate and persist within the viscid airway mucus rather than being cleared. Fungal antigens provoke a vigorous combined type I (IgE-mediated) and type III (immune-complex) hypersensitivity response, with strong Th2 activation, eosinophil recruitment, and high IgE production. The resulting intense airway inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and mucoid impaction damage the bronchial walls, leading to central bronchiectasis. Recurrent inflammatory episodes can ultimately produce fibrosis and irreversible loss of lung function.
additionalDifferentials: Invasive or semi-invasive aspergillosis and aspergilloma
additionalInvestigations: Total serum IgE, which is characteristically very high and useful for monitoring
Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG (precipitins) and skin testing for sensitisation
High-resolution CT to detect central bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction
Sputum examination for Aspergillus and eosinophils
redFlags: Progressive fixed airflow obstruction or fibrosis indicating advanced disease
Frequent severe asthma exacerbations unresponsive to standard therapy
Features suggesting invasive aspergillosis in an immunocompromised patient
Massive mucoid impaction causing lobar collapse
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and appropriate immunosuppressive treatment, exacerbations can be controlled and lung damage limited; however, repeated undertreated flares lead to progressive bronchiectasis and fibrosis with permanent loss of lung function, so long-term monitoring of symptoms and IgE is important.
pitfalls: Mistaking ABPA for ordinary difficult asthma and missing the diagnosis
Confusing this hypersensitivity condition with invasive aspergillosis and mismanaging treatment
Failing to monitor total IgE to gauge disease activity and treatment response
Overlooking ABPA as a treatable cause of bronchiectasis
